My growing guide wrote the roadmap for my analytics tool

October 23, 2026•code

In March I wrote about Puls, my own cookieless analytics in a single PHP file. Since then it has gone from 1.0 to 1.26. A lot of that happened in a few days in October, and almost all of it because of Odlingsguiden.

Every event is a question

When we decided to work more data driven with Odlingsguiden, I set one rule. Every event we send has to answer a question we actually have.

Do people choose their growing zone? zone_set. Do they finish the guides? guide_finished. What do they search for that we don’t have? search_miss. Do they use Min odling? plant_added, plant_removed, note_saved.

About fifteen named events. Not “track everything and look later”. That never happens anyway.

Puls already had custom events since the spring. But once I started asking real questions, it couldn’t answer most of them. So I wrote down what was missing and went over to the Puls repo.

The bug that ate search queries

First thing I found was a bug. Puls dedupes events, so the same event from the same visitor within 10 seconds only counts once. Makes sense for double clicks.

But the dedup key ignored the event data. So if someone searched for two different things that both missed, only the first search_miss was kept. The exact data I wanted the most was silently thrown away.

Now the data is part of the key.

Things the guide needed

Here’s roughly what Puls got, in the order Odlingsguiden asked for it:

  1. A queue stub, so puls.track() calls made before the script has loaded aren’t lost.
  2. data-debug on the script tag, which logs every event to the console. Beacons are fire and forget, so before this there was no way to see from the browser what Puls actually received.
  3. A drill-down per event. A trend over time, and group by any key in the event data. So search_miss grouped by query shows exactly what people miss.
  4. Two-step funnels. Of the people who did A, how many went on to do B the same day?
  5. Goals that can be an event, not just a page.
  6. An app version on every hit with data-version. The day a new version is first seen gets a marker on the chart. So when we shipped the new start page I could see the line where it went out.
  7. Saved breakdowns as their own cards on the dashboard.
  8. Events kept for 400 days instead of 90.

That last one is my favourite. A growing guide is seasonal. Comparing October with September tells you nothing. You need to compare this spring with last spring. 90 days of history would never get you there.

Funnels got slow

The first version of the funnel ran a lookup per visitor. On a test database with 500,000 events, a 30-day funnel took 25 seconds.

Rewrote it as a join against a per-visitor aggregate of the second event. Same result, verified row by row, and the cost basically disappeared.

A report I don’t have to open a dashboard for

Odlingsguiden has an npm run puls:report script now. It fetches traffic, goals and all events with groupings and funnels through a share token, and writes it all to a markdown file in the repo.

So once a month there’s a snapshot I can read, compare with the last one and actually make decisions from. Without logging into anything.

The second round

After the first week of real data, Odlingsguiden had three more wishes:

  • Chart notes. One Saturday had a spike that didn’t show up as any source. A film about our farm had come out, and apps don’t send a referrer. Now you can mark a date with “Film came out” and see it on the chart later.
  • Bounce rate per entry page. Not just for the whole site. Which pages do people land on and leave?
  • More than ten events in the API. Odlingsguiden already sends more than that.

All three are in Puls 1.22.

Building the tool you need

This is the fun part of owning your tools. When something is missing you just build it. And because it’s open source, everyone else who runs Puls gets it too.

Puls is on GitHub, MIT licensed, still one PHP file.
